position: attributive only — alone (*induced labor*); in compounds also after a verb: *The headaches are stress-induced*
form: -ed from *induce*; very often the second half of a compound: *drug-induced*, *stress-induced*

senses.gloss: Caused on purpose by doctors or drugs, or caused by the thing named in a compound.
examples: The doctors kept him in an *induced* coma for three days.
She had an *induced* labor because the baby was two weeks late.
Many of his health problems are *stress-induced*.

senses.gloss: Letting someone have or do whatever they want, often too kindly.
examples: Her grandparents are much more *indulgent* than her parents.
He gave his son an *indulgent* smile and let him stay up late.
Some teachers think today's parents are too *indulgent*.

senses.gloss: Rich and pleasant in a way that feels like a special treat.
examples: We finished with an *indulgent* chocolate cake.
A long bath on a weeknight feels wonderfully *indulgent*.

senses.gloss: Strong enough to be used in factories or for heavy work.
examples: You'll need *industrial-strength* glue to fix that.
The cleaner is *industrial-strength*, so wear gloves.

senses.gloss: Informal: very strong or intense.
examples: He makes *industrial-strength* coffee every morning.
It took an *industrial-strength* effort to get the bill passed.

senses.gloss: Having a lot of industry and factories.
examples: Obesity rates are rising in most *industrialized* countries.
The north of the country is heavily *industrialized*.
The US was one of the most *industrialized* nations in the world by 1900.

senses.gloss: Formal or humorous: drunk.
examples: The driver was clearly *inebriated* when police stopped him.
An *inebriated* guest fell into the pool.
By midnight, the best man was more *inebriated* than the groom.

senses.gloss: Not fit to eat, because it is bad, badly cooked or poisonous.
examples: The steak was so overcooked it was *inedible*.
Some of these mushrooms are *inedible*, so don't pick them.
The cafeteria served an almost *inedible* meatloaf.

senses.gloss: Not producing the result that was wanted.
examples: Antibiotics are *ineffective* against viruses.
The new law has been largely *ineffective*.
The second treatment was even more *ineffective* than the first.

contrast: *ineffectual* usually describes a person who is weak and cannot get things done (*an ineffectual leader*); for a method, drug or law, *ineffective* is the everyday word.

senses.gloss: Not able to get things done or produce results; weak.
examples: Critics called him an *ineffectual* leader.
Her attempts to calm the crowd were *ineffectual*.
The committee became more *ineffectual* every year.

contrast: Russian *неэффективный* covers two words: *ineffective* — it does not work; *inefficient* — it works, but wastes time, money or energy.

senses.gloss: Wasting time, money or energy; not working in the best way.
examples: Old refrigerators are very *inefficient* and use a lot of electricity.
The billing system is slow and *inefficient*.
It's the most *inefficient* way to heat a house.

senses.gloss: Not graceful, attractive or well done; clumsy.
examples: It's an *inelegant* solution, but it works.
He landed in the water with an *inelegant* splash.
The new logo is even more *inelegant* than the old one.

ru: не имеющий права, не соответствующий условиям

senses.gloss: Not allowed to have or do something because you do not meet the rules.
examples: Students who miss the deadline are *ineligible* for financial aid.
He was *ineligible* to vote because he was only seventeen.
The team used an *ineligible* player and lost the game by forfeit.

senses.gloss: Having no skill; doing something badly.
examples: The robbers were so *inept* that they locked themselves out of the getaway car.
I'm totally *inept* at fixing things around the house.
It was the most *inept* response to a crisis I've ever seen.

senses.gloss: Formal: not fair, especially in the way money or chances are shared.
examples: Critics say the tax system is *inequitable*.
The report describes an *inequitable* distribution of school funding.
The new rules made an already unfair system even more *inequitable*.

comparison: more/most — *more inert* (the 'not moving' sense); the chemistry sense is not gradable

senses.gloss: Not moving or acting; without energy or life.
examples: The man lay *inert* on the sidewalk until the paramedics arrived.
The economy has been *inert* for months.
The market was even more *inert* than analysts had predicted.

senses.gloss: Of a substance, not reacting with other chemicals.
examples: Helium is an *inert* gas.
The pill contains active ingredients and some *inert* fillers.

senses.gloss: Impossible to avoid or ignore.
examples: The conclusion is *inescapable*: the plan failed.
Social media has become an *inescapable* part of teenage life.
In August, the heat in Phoenix is *inescapable*.

contrast: *the inevitable* is also a noun — what cannot be avoided: *We tried to delay the inevitable*.

senses.gloss: Certain to happen; impossible to prevent.
examples: Some mistakes are *inevitable* when you're learning.
It was *inevitable* that the two companies would merge.
After the scandal, his resignation was almost *inevitable*.

senses.gloss: Not completely accurate or correct.
examples: Predicting the weather is still an *inexact* science.
The translation is a little *inexact*.
Older methods of dating fossils were far more *inexact*.

senses.gloss: Too bad to be forgiven or explained away.
examples: His behavior at the wedding was *inexcusable*.
Losing the patient's records was an *inexcusable* mistake.
It's completely *inexcusable* to leave a dog in a hot car.

senses.gloss: So large that it can never be used up.
examples: The sun is an almost *inexhaustible* source of energy.
Her patience with the kids seemed *inexhaustible*.

senses.gloss: Of a person, never getting tired.
examples: He was an *inexhaustible* campaigner for civil rights.
At eighty, she is still *inexhaustible*.

senses.gloss: Formal: impossible to stop or change.
examples: Nothing could stop the *inexorable* rise in prices.
The decline of the small town seemed *inexorable*.
They watched the *inexorable* advance of the flood waters.

contrast: *inexpensive* sounds more positive than *cheap*, which can also mean 'of poor quality': *an inexpensive hotel* is a good deal; *a cheap hotel* may be a bad one.

senses.gloss: Not costing a lot of money.
examples: We found an *inexpensive* little restaurant near the beach.
Rice and beans are healthy and *inexpensive*.
This is one of the most *inexpensive* ways to insulate your home.

senses.gloss: Having little knowledge or skill because you have not done something much.
examples: The team is young and *inexperienced*.
An *inexperienced* driver should not be out in this snow.
She was the most *inexperienced* candidate in the race.

senses.gloss: Impossible to explain or understand.
examples: For some *inexplicable* reason, the printer only works on Tuesdays.
His sudden decision to quit was *inexplicable*.
The lights went out for an *inexplicable* ten minutes.

senses.gloss: Never wrong or never making mistakes.
examples: Doctors aren't *infallible*.
He speaks as if his judgment were *infallible*.

senses.gloss: Always working or giving the right result.
examples: There's no *infallible* way to pick stocks.
Grandma had an *infallible* cure for hiccups.

form: in- + *famous*, but stressed on the first syllable
contrast: *infamous* does not mean 'not famous' — it means famous for something bad. The stress moves: *IN-famous*, not *in-FAMOUS*.

senses.gloss: Well known for something bad.
examples: Alcatraz was an *infamous* prison in San Francisco Bay.
The highway is *infamous* for its traffic jams.
He was one of the most *infamous* gangsters of the 1920s.

senses.gloss: Disapproving: behaving in a silly way, like a small child.
examples: Stop being so *infantile* and apologize.
The show's humor gets more *infantile* every season.

senses.gloss: Medical: affecting babies or very young children.
examples: Polio used to be called *infantile* paralysis.
The clinic treats *infantile* eczema.

senses.gloss: Having a strong, usually short-lived love for someone or something.
examples: He's completely *infatuated* with the new girl in his class.
The *infatuated* teenager wrote her name all over his notebook.
She grew more *infatuated* with the city every time she visited.

senses.gloss: Formal: not possible or practical to do.
examples: Building a bridge there is economically *infeasible*.
The engineers rejected the design as *infeasible*.
A two-week deadline is simply *infeasible* for a project this size.

senses.gloss: Of a wound or body part, full of germs, so that it is red, swollen and sore.
examples: The cut on his hand got *infected*.
She had an *infected* tooth pulled.

senses.gloss: Of a person or animal, carrying a disease.
examples: *Infected* patients were kept in a separate ward.
Thousands of people were *infected* with the virus.

senses.gloss: Of a computer or file, containing a virus.
examples: Don't open attachments from *infected* accounts.
My laptop is *infected*, so I'm using my phone.

senses.gloss: Of a disease, spread by germs; of a person, able to pass a disease to others.
examples: Measles is one of the most *infectious* diseases known.
You're still *infectious*, so stay home for a few days.
She works in the *infectious* disease unit.

senses.gloss: Of a feeling or laugh, quickly spreading to other people.
examples: He has an *infectious* laugh.
Her enthusiasm was *infectious*.

senses.gloss: Old-fashioned, informal: very annoying.
examples: Turn off that *infernal* noise!
I spent an hour trying to fix this *infernal* machine.

senses.gloss: Literary: of or like hell.
examples: Dante describes the *infernal* regions in great detail.
The furnace room gave off an *infernal* heat.

senses.gloss: Of a person or animal, not able to have babies or young.
examples: They were told they were *infertile* and decided to adopt.
Some *infertile* couples try IVF.

senses.gloss: Of land or soil, not good for growing plants.
examples: The soil here is rocky and *infertile*.
Farmers abandoned the *infertile* land decades ago.

senses.gloss: Extremely small.
examples: The water contained an *infinitesimal* amount of lead.
The chances of winning the lottery are *infinitesimal*.
The difference in price was *infinitesimal*.

contrast: *the infirm* is used as a plural noun — people who are weak or ill: *care for the elderly and the infirm*.

senses.gloss: Weak or ill, especially because of old age.
examples: She looks after her elderly and *infirm* father.
The nursing home is for *infirm* patients who need daily care.
He became more *infirm* after the fall.

senses.gloss: Of a part of the body, red, hot, swollen and painful.
examples: His knee was badly *inflamed*.
She has *inflamed* gums.
The rash looked more *inflamed* the next morning.

senses.gloss: Full of strong feelings, especially anger.
examples: The speech was aimed at an already *inflamed* crowd.
Tempers were *inflamed* after the referee's call.

comparison: more/most — *more inflammatory* (the 'causing anger' sense); the medical sense is not gradable

senses.gloss: Likely to make people angry or violent.
examples: The senator was criticized for his *inflammatory* remarks.
Her latest post was even more *inflammatory* than the last one.

senses.gloss: Medical: causing or connected with inflammation.
examples: Arthritis is an *inflammatory* disease of the joints.
Take an *anti-inflammatory* drug for the swelling.

contrast: *an inflatable* is also a noun — an inflatable boat or toy.

senses.gloss: Able to be filled with air.
examples: The kids spent all day on an *inflatable* raft.
We slept on an *inflatable* mattress in the living room.
The bounce house is *inflatable* and packs into a small bag.

senses.gloss: Higher, bigger or more important than is true or reasonable.
examples: Tourists pay *inflated* prices near the stadium.
He has an *inflated* opinion of himself.
Home prices here are even more *inflated* than in the city.

senses.gloss: Filled with air or gas.
examples: Make sure the tires are properly *inflated*.
The room was full of *inflated* balloons.

senses.gloss: Causing or connected with a general rise in prices.
examples: Some economists warned that the tax cuts would be *inflationary*.
The country went through a long *inflationary* period.
Rising wages can add to *inflationary* pressure.

senses.gloss: Of rules or people, unwilling or unable to change.
examples: The school has an *inflexible* attendance policy.
My boss is completely *inflexible* about working from home.
The rules became more *inflexible* under the new manager.

senses.gloss: Of a material, stiff and not able to bend.
examples: The old plastic had become brittle and *inflexible*.
These boots have an *inflexible* sole.

senses.gloss: Having a lot of power to change what people think or do.
examples: She was *influential* in getting the law changed.
His father is an *influential* lawyer in Chicago.
The Beatles were among the most *influential* bands of all time.

senses.gloss: Not official; not following the usual rules or procedures.
examples: We had an *informal* meeting over coffee.
The two countries reached an *informal* agreement.

senses.gloss: Relaxed and friendly, not ceremonial; of clothes, casual.
examples: The dinner is *informal*, so jeans are fine.
The new office has a much more *informal* atmosphere.

senses.gloss: Of words or style, used in everyday conversation rather than in serious writing.
examples: *Kid* is an *informal* word for *child*.
Your essay is too *informal* for a college application.

contrast: *informational* says what something is for (*an informational meeting* — held to give information); *informative* says it actually taught you something (*a very informative meeting*).

senses.gloss: Meant to give people information.
examples: The college holds an *informational* session for parents every fall.
She picked up an *informational* brochure at the clinic.
He set up an *informational* interview with someone in the industry.

senses.gloss: Giving useful or interesting information.
examples: Thanks for the talk — it was very *informative*.
The museum has an *informative* audio guide.
Her second article was even more *informative* than the first.

senses.gloss: Knowing a lot about a subject or about what is happening.
examples: Voters need to stay *informed* about the issues.
Please keep me *informed*.
Readers today are more *informed* than ever.

senses.gloss: Based on good information.
examples: Read the reviews so you can make an *informed* decision.
My guess is only a partly *informed* guess.

senses.gloss: Of light, just beyond red in the spectrum, so that people cannot see it.
examples: The camera uses *infrared* light to see in the dark.
The TV remote sends an *infrared* signal.
This kind of radiation is *infrared*, so you feel it as heat.

senses.gloss: Not happening often.
examples: Buses to the airport are *infrequent* on Sundays.
He made *infrequent* visits to his hometown.
Her calls became more and more *infrequent*.

form: -ed — the person who feels it; from *infuriate*
contrast: *infuriated* is how you feel; *infuriating* is what makes you feel it: *I was infuriated by the infuriating delay*.

senses.gloss: Extremely angry.
examples: Fans were *infuriated* by the ticket prices.
An *infuriated* customer demanded to see the manager.
She was even more *infuriated* when he laughed.

contrast: *infuriating* is what makes you angry; *infuriated* is how you feel.

senses.gloss: Making you extremely angry.
examples: It's *infuriating* when the Wi-Fi drops in the middle of a call.
He has an *infuriating* habit of interrupting.
The most *infuriating* part was that nobody apologized.

contrast: Do not confuse with *ingenuous* (naive, trusting). *ingenious* is about clever ideas: *an ingenious plan*.

senses.gloss: Very clever and original, especially in solving a problem.
examples: What an *ingenious* idea!
She came up with an *ingenious* way to store bikes in a tiny apartment.
It's one of the most *ingenious* inventions of the century.

contrast: Do not confuse with *ingenious* (clever). *ingenuous* means honest and trusting, sometimes too much so.

senses.gloss: Honest, open and trusting, sometimes in a naive way.
examples: It was an *ingenuous* question, and nobody laughed at her.
He's too *ingenuous* to lie about it.
She seemed more *ingenuous* than the other candidates.

senses.gloss: Of a habit or belief, so fixed that it is hard to change.
examples: Racism was deeply *ingrained* in the town's culture.
Bad habits get more *ingrained* the longer you keep them.
Saving money is an *ingrained* habit for her.

senses.gloss: Of dirt, pressed deeply into a surface.
examples: His hands were rough, with *ingrained* grease.
No cleaner could get the *ingrained* dirt out of the carpet.

senses.gloss: Trying too hard to make people like you.
examples: The waiter gave us an *ingratiating* smile.
His tone was polite, almost *ingratiating*.
The new intern is even more *ingratiating* than the last one.

contrast: US *an ingrown toenail*; British English says *an ingrowing toenail*.

senses.gloss: Of a nail or hair, growing into the skin.
examples: He went to the podiatrist with an *ingrown* toenail.
Shaving too close can cause *ingrown* hairs.
An *ingrown* nail can get infected if you ignore it.

senses.gloss: Having people or animals living there.
examples: Only two of the islands are *inhabited*.
It's one of the oldest continuously *inhabited* cities in the world.
The house looked *inhabited*, but nobody answered the door.

position: both — also right after a noun with *in*: *the risks inherent in the job*

senses.gloss: Being a natural, basic part of something that cannot be removed.
examples: There are risks *inherent* in any surgery.
The design has an *inherent* flaw.
Some danger is *inherent* in extreme sports.

senses.gloss: Received from someone who has died.
examples: They lived on *inherited* money.
The furniture is mostly *inherited* from her grandparents.

senses.gloss: Passed from parents to children through the genes.
examples: Cystic fibrosis is an *inherited* disease.
Some forms of high cholesterol are *inherited*.

senses.gloss: Too embarrassed or nervous to act or speak freely.
examples: He feels *inhibited* speaking English in front of native speakers.
She was a shy, *inhibited* child.
People are usually more *inhibited* around their bosses.

senses.gloss: Of a place, hard to live in or travel through.
examples: Antarctica is the most *inhospitable* place on earth.
They crossed a hot, *inhospitable* desert.

senses.gloss: Of a person, unfriendly to visitors.
examples: The locals were not *inhospitable*, just shy.
It would be *inhospitable* not to offer them dinner.

contrast: *inhuman* means extremely cruel or not like a human (*an inhuman scream*); *inhumane* is about treatment that causes needless suffering (*inhumane conditions*).

senses.gloss: Extremely cruel, without any pity.
examples: The prisoners suffered *inhuman* treatment.
It was the most *inhuman* act of the whole war.

senses.gloss: Not seeming human; strange and frightening.
examples: An *inhuman* scream came from the woods.
The runner kept up an almost *inhuman* pace.

contrast: Not the same as *inhuman*: *inhumane* describes treatment or conditions that cause needless suffering to people or animals.

senses.gloss: Causing people or animals to suffer in a way that is not acceptable.
examples: Activists protested the *inhumane* treatment of farm animals.
Conditions in the detention center were *inhumane*.
Solitary confinement is one of the most *inhumane* punishments.

position: both — mostly before a noun, often after a possessive: *in her own inimitable style*

senses.gloss: So special or unusual that no one can copy it.
examples: She told the story in her own *inimitable* way.
Nobody sings like him — his voice is *inimitable*.
The film is full of the director's *inimitable* humor.

contrast: *initials* (noun) are the first letters of your names; *to initial* (verb) means to sign with them.

senses.gloss: Happening at the beginning; first.
examples: My *initial* reaction was to say no.
The *initial* cost is high, but you save money later.
After the *initial* shock, she handled the news well.

contrast: *injectables* (noun, plural) are drugs given by injection, especially cosmetic ones.

senses.gloss: Able to be given with a needle.
examples: The vaccine comes in an *injectable* form.
Some weight-loss drugs are only *injectable*.
Her doctor switched her to an *injectable* medication.

senses.gloss: Decorated with pieces of wood, metal or stone set into the surface.
examples: They ate at an old table *inlaid* with mother-of-pearl.
The box has an *inlaid* wooden lid.
The floor is *inlaid* with marble tiles.

contrast: After a verb, *inland* is an adverb with the stress often on the second syllable: *They moved inland*. The adjective only goes before a noun: *an inland city*.

senses.gloss: In the middle of a country, far from the sea.
examples: Salt Lake City is an *inland* city.
Lake Superior is the largest *inland* lake in North America.
The storm brought heavy rain to *inland* areas.

senses.gloss: Present from birth, not learned.
examples: She has an *innate* sense of rhythm.
Is the ability to learn language *innate*?
Babies have an *innate* fear of falling.

comparison: not gradable — it is already a superlative form

senses.gloss: Most private and personal.
examples: She wrote her *innermost* thoughts in a diary.
He never shared his *innermost* feelings with anyone.

senses.gloss: Closest to the center.
examples: The *innermost* room of the temple is closed to visitors.
Mercury is the *innermost* planet.

senses.gloss: Not harmful or offensive.
examples: It was an *innocuous* question, but she got upset.
The snake looks dangerous, but it's completely *innocuous*.
Even the most *innocuous* joke can offend someone.

senses.gloss: Using new methods or ideas.
examples: The company is known for its *innovative* designs.
Her approach to teaching math is very *innovative*.
It was voted the most *innovative* startup of the year.

position: both — mostly before a plural noun

senses.gloss: Too many to count.
examples: I've told him *innumerable* times to lock the door.
The sky was full of *innumerable* stars.
The problems with the plan are *innumerable*.

senses.gloss: Not likely to upset or annoy anyone; sometimes, too plain to be interesting.
examples: He's a quiet, *inoffensive* man.
The hotel was decorated in *inoffensive* beige.
They chose the most *inoffensive* song they could find for the ad.

senses.gloss: Medical: not able to be treated or removed by surgery.
examples: He was diagnosed with an *inoperable* brain tumor.
The cancer had spread and was *inoperable*.

senses.gloss: Of a machine or system, not working or not able to be used.
examples: The runway was *inoperable* after the storm.
A power failure left the elevators *inoperable*.

senses.gloss: Formal: happening at a bad time.
examples: The phone rang at an *inopportune* moment.
His timing could not have been more *inopportune*.
Is this an *inopportune* time to ask about a raise?

senses.gloss: Much more than is usual or reasonable.
examples: He spends an *inordinate* amount of time on his phone.
The project caused an *inordinate* delay.
She takes an *inordinate* interest in her neighbors' lives.

contrast: Used in science. For food grown with chemicals, Americans say *conventional* or *nonorganic*, not *inorganic*.

senses.gloss: Not made of living things or of carbon compounds.
examples: Rocks and metals are *inorganic* materials.
She's taking a course in *inorganic* chemistry.
The fertilizer is *inorganic*, made from minerals.

contrast: American spelling is *inquiring*; British English often writes *enquiring*.

senses.gloss: Always wanting to learn and find things out.
examples: Scientists need an *inquiring* mind.
She was the most *inquiring* student in the class.

senses.gloss: Of a look or voice, showing that you want to ask something.
examples: He gave me an *inquiring* look.
She raised an *inquiring* eyebrow.

senses.gloss: Wanting to know about things, sometimes too much about other people's business.
examples: Cats are *inquisitive* animals.
Our *inquisitive* neighbor asked how much we paid for the house.
Kids get more *inquisitive* as they learn to talk.

contrast: In the sense 'mentally ill', *insane* is now mostly a legal or old-fashioned word; doctors say *mentally ill*. In everyday speech it usually means 'crazy' or 'amazing'.

senses.gloss: Very foolish or dangerous; crazy.
examples: You'd be *insane* to drive in this snow.
Quitting a good job was an *insane* idea.
That's the most *insane* thing I've ever heard.

senses.gloss: Informal: extreme or amazing.
examples: The traffic this morning was *insane*.
The view from the top is *insane*.

senses.gloss: Legal or old-fashioned: seriously mentally ill.
examples: The jury found him *insane* and not responsible for the crime.
The hospital was built for the criminally *insane*.

senses.gloss: Always wanting more and never satisfied.
examples: The public has an *insatiable* appetite for celebrity gossip.
As a kid, his curiosity was *insatiable*.
She's an *insatiable* reader.

senses.gloss: Impossible to understand, especially what someone is thinking or feeling.
examples: The poker player kept an *inscrutable* face.
Her reasons for leaving remain *inscrutable*.
The instructions were even more *inscrutable* than the software.

senses.gloss: Not confident about yourself or your abilities.
examples: Many teenagers feel *insecure* about their looks.
He's more *insecure* than he seems.

senses.gloss: Not safe or protected; likely to fail or be lost.
examples: Don't enter your password on an *insecure* network.
Millions of workers have *insecure* jobs.

senses.gloss: Not noticing or caring how other people feel.
examples: That was a really *insensitive* thing to say.
The company was accused of being *insensitive* to its workers' needs.
It was the most *insensitive* joke of the night.

senses.gloss: Not physically affected by something.
examples: Some people are *insensitive* to pain.
This kind of film is *insensitive* to light.

senses.gloss: Of people, always together because they are very close.
examples: The two sisters are *inseparable*.
They've been *inseparable* friends since kindergarten.

senses.gloss: Of things, so closely connected that they cannot be separated.
examples: For him, freedom is *inseparable* from responsibility.
Music is an *inseparable* part of the culture.

contrast: *inside* is most often a preposition or adverb (*inside the box*, *come inside*) or a noun (*the inside of the car*); the adjective only goes before a noun.

senses.gloss: On or in the inner part of something.
examples: He keeps his wallet in an *inside* pocket.
Slower traffic should use the *inside* lane.

senses.gloss: Known by or done by people within a group or organization.
examples: The police think the robbery was an *inside* job.
She had *inside* information about the merger.

senses.gloss: Harmful in a slow, hidden way that is hard to notice.
examples: High blood pressure is an *insidious* disease.
The effects of the propaganda were *insidious*.
Everyday prejudice can be more *insidious* than open hate.

senses.gloss: Showing a clear, deep understanding of a person or situation.
examples: She made some very *insightful* comments about the book.
It's an *insightful* look at life in a small town.
His second book is far more *insightful* than his first.

senses.gloss: Too small or unimportant to matter.
examples: The difference in price is *insignificant*.
Standing next to the Grand Canyon makes you feel *insignificant*.
They argued over the most *insignificant* details.

senses.gloss: Pretending to feel something that you do not really feel.
examples: His apology sounded *insincere*.
She gave me an *insincere* smile.
Politicians often seem more *insincere* on TV than in person.

senses.gloss: Of food or drink, having almost no taste.
examples: The soup was watery and *insipid*.
Supermarket tomatoes are often *insipid*.

senses.gloss: Dull and boring, with no strong character.
examples: The movie has an *insipid* script.
It was the most *insipid* pop song of the summer.

senses.gloss: Demanding something firmly and not accepting no.
examples: She was *insistent* that we stay for dinner.
He's very *insistent* on paying for everything.
The calls from the bank got more *insistent*.

senses.gloss: Of a sound or feeling, continuing and hard to ignore.
examples: I woke up to the *insistent* ringing of the phone.
There was an *insistent* knocking at the door.

senses.gloss: Rude and not showing respect, especially to someone in authority.
examples: The student was suspended for being *insolent* to a teacher.
He gave the officer an *insolent* stare.
Her answers grew more *insolent* with every question.

contrast: For a problem, American English more often says *unsolvable*; *insoluble* is mostly used for substances.

senses.gloss: Of a substance, not able to dissolve in a liquid.
examples: Oil is *insoluble* in water.
Beans are a good source of *insoluble* fiber.

senses.gloss: Of a problem, impossible to solve.
examples: The conflict seemed *insoluble*.
They faced an almost *insoluble* dilemma.

senses.gloss: Formal: not having enough money to pay debts.
examples: The airline was declared *insolvent* last year.
Several *insolvent* banks were taken over by the government.
Without a loan, the company will be *insolvent* by March.

senses.gloss: Giving people hope, energy or the wish to do something good.
examples: The coach gave an *inspirational* speech before the game.
Her story of recovery is truly *inspirational*.
He was the most *inspirational* teacher I ever had.

contrast: *an instant* (noun) is a very short moment: *for an instant*. *Instantly* is the adverb.

senses.gloss: Happening immediately.
examples: The show was an *instant* success.
Members get *instant* access to all videos.
The two dogs became *instant* friends.

senses.gloss: Of food or drink, very quick to prepare, usually by adding hot water.
examples: In college, I lived on *instant* noodles.
Is this real coffee or *instant* coffee?

contrast: *instantaneous* is more formal or technical; in everyday speech *instant* is more common.

senses.gloss: Happening immediately, with no delay at all.
examples: The effect of the drug is almost *instantaneous*.
Death was *instantaneous*.
The app gives *instantaneous* translations.

senses.gloss: Done or felt without thinking, by natural reaction.
examples: My *instinctive* reaction was to duck.
For a mother bear, protecting her cubs is *instinctive*.
She's a more *instinctive* player than her sister.

comparison: not gradable — the 'dull, impersonal' sense can take *more*

senses.gloss: Belonging to or done by a large organization, such as a bank, school or government.
examples: *Institutional* investors own most of the company's shares.
The report describes *institutional* racism in the police department.

senses.gloss: Plain, dull and impersonal, like a hospital or prison.
examples: The dorm rooms had an *institutional* look.
The food was bland and *institutional*.

ru: узаконенный, укоренившийся; привыкший к жизни в учреждении

senses.gloss: Of a practice, made a fixed part of an organization or society.
examples: Segregation was *institutionalized* in the South for decades.
Corruption has become more *institutionalized* over the years.

senses.gloss: Of a person, so used to life in a prison or hospital that they cannot live independently.
examples: After thirty years in prison, he was completely *institutionalized*.
Many *institutionalized* patients struggled when the hospital closed.
